summary: Rival claims over who controls Hormuz, a heavy Russian strike on Ukraine's grid, France's worst riots in years, China's draft AI export curbs, Sudan at the UN and Israel's tight race.

topics.heading: US and Iran both claim control of Hormuz as Iran says a supertanker hit a mine
topics.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say a supertanker hit a mine on "unauthorised" routes; the US says it controls the strait and that ships are being hit by Iranian projectiles. A UK monitor counted at least 12 attacks in a week and says the true number is likely higher.

lead.title: US and Iran both claim control of Strait of Hormuz amid attacks on vessels

alsoReported.title: Super tanker ablaze after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz, IRGC says

article: On Saturday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude caught fire after hitting a sea mine while using an "unauthorised" route through the Strait of Hormuz[^1][^2]. It accused the ship of switching off its tracking systems. Euronews notes the location is unclear and the footage has not been independently checked[^2].

The two sides tell very different stories. US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moved through the strait last week, and that it is "controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran"[^1]. The US says it has cleared the mines and that ships are being struck by projectiles; it says a container ship that sank this week, the GFS Pride, was hit by one, not by a mine as Iran said[^1]. Iran says the US is inflating its numbers, and that ships must coordinate with a new Iranian strait authority[^1].

Some numbers come from outside both governments. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) counted at least 12 attacks in the week to October 16, but warned that many ships do not report to it[^1]. Data firm Kpler estimates oil flows were about 68% of the pre-war level in the week to October 13[^1]. Brent crude touched $110 a barrel on Friday[^1].

Why it matters: about a quarter of the world's seaborne oil normally passes through this strait, so who controls it shows up in fuel prices worldwide, including in Canada[^2]. The US has not hit back for the recent attacks. US media report that Trump has told the military to be ready for larger strikes after the November 3 midterms, while Pakistan and Qatar keep passing messages[^1]. My read: the gap between the two sides' claims is itself a sign that neither can fully secure the route.
topics.differences: The US says it controls the strait, has cleared mines and that Iran is firing at ships out of "desperation"; Iran says ships are hitting mines on routes it has not approved and that US traffic figures are exaggerated[^1][^2]. Neither side's numbers have been independently confirmed; UKMTO says its own count is incomplete[^1].

topics.heading: Russia hits Ukraine's power grid in one of the war's largest energy attacks
topics.summary: Russian drones and missiles struck more than 15 power sites, Ukraine says, killing 7 to 8 people and leaving over a million without electricity. The UN says civilian deaths in 2026 are far above last year's.

lead.title: Russian attacks in Ukraine kill at least 8, cut power to 1 million

alsoReported.title: Russia launches 'one of its largest attacks' on Ukraine's energy grid as US 'disregards' Graham's sanctions, Zelensky says

article: Russia launched a large drone and missile attack on Ukraine on Friday night into Saturday. Ukraine's air force said it downed 289 of 332 drones, and that drones and ballistic missiles hit 22 locations[^4]. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it one of the largest strikes on the energy system, aimed at more than 15 power generation and transmission sites[^4].

The death toll differs by count and time window. Al Jazeera, citing Ukrainian officials, reports at least eight killed and 60 injured across nine regions on Friday; the Kyiv Independent reports seven killed and about 90 injured over the past day[^3][^4]. Power was cut to more than a million people, most of whom had it back by Saturday, though some western cities near Poland were told blackouts could last a day or more[^3]. Russia's military chief told President Vladimir Putin the army had what it needs to keep up the campaign against Ukraine's grid[^3].

Background: since 2022, Russia has struck Ukraine's power system each autumn and winter, when people need heat and light most. A US-announced pause on energy strikes collapsed last week. Zelenskyy criticised Washington for setting aside a sanctions bill backed by Senator Lindsey Graham, and said concessions to Moscow encourage more attacks[^4].

Why it matters: the UN human rights mission says at least 2,570 civilians were killed in Ukraine from January to September 2026, almost 60% more than in the same months of 2025[^3]. Its head said the first two weeks of October were "among the deadliest periods for civilians in years"[^3]. My read: with talks stalled, the coming winter is likely to be a contest over the power grid, which is why Ukraine keeps asking Europe for air defence.

topics.heading: Hundreds of thousands march across France over living costs and schools
topics.summary: Students, unions and revived "yellow vest" groups marched in many cities. Most marches were peaceful, but riots hit Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges, and the prime minister said about 1,200 people were arrested.

lead.title: Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years

alsoReported.title: Protests erupt across France against rising living costs and in support of students

article: Reuters described Saturday's protests in France as the country's worst riots in years, though most people marched peacefully. The interior minister put turnout at about 550,000 across the country; the CGT union, one of the organisers, said 800,000[^5]. People marched against rising living costs and fuel prices and in support of high school students who have been protesting since September[^5][^6]. Calls on social media to revive the 2018 "yellow vest" movement added to the crowds[^6].

Violence broke out in several cities. Reuters reports Limoges city hall was set on fire, Marseille's city hall was broken into, and shops and banks were attacked in Paris[^5]. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said about 1,200 people were arrested and more than 150 police officers injured, and blamed the "ultra-left" and criminals[^5]. A police watchdog is looking into at least two dozen complaints of police violence[^5].

Background: the student movement began on September 21, when pupils in poorer parts of Paris boycotted classes over unreplaced teachers, crowded classes and run-down buildings[^7]. It grew alongside public-sector strikes against a 2027 budget plan that would cut about €54 billion in spending, including a pay freeze for public workers[^7]. Weeks of clashes have led to thousands of arrests, and a 15-year-old lost a hand to a police stun grenade; the interior minister has since suspended that type of grenade[^6][^7].

Why it matters: France is trying to cut a large deficit while prices rise, and the protests are now shaping the presidential campaign[^6]. President Emmanuel Macron promised to punish those behind the attacks[^5]. My read: the key question is whether the government's promised response to students' demands can separate the peaceful majority from the violent fringe.
topics.differences: Turnout figures differ: about 550,000 according to the interior minister, 800,000 according to the CGT union[^5]. The government blames the ultra-left and criminals for the violence; protesters say most marchers were peaceful and troublemakers were to blame, and rights groups have criticised police force used against minors[^5][^7].

topics.heading: China drafts export controls on its most advanced AI models and chip designs
topics.summary: Two Chinese ministries proposed restricting exports of 40 technologies, 23 of them in AI, including very large models and some chip designs. Comments are open until November 15; a temporary registration rule is already in force.

lead.title: China moves to curb tech exports, including AI, citing national security risks

alsoReported.title: China proposes export controls on its advanced AI models and chip designs

article: On Friday, China's commerce and science ministries published a draft update to the list of technologies that need permission to be exported, or cannot be exported at all[^8]. It covers 40 items: 23 in AI, 12 in solar power, including polysilicon manufacturing, and 5 in biomedicine, such as gene therapy[^8][^9].

The AI part is the most watched. It would cover the core parts of large models, such as model weights (the learned numbers that make a model work) and source code, for models with at least 2 trillion parameters or that rank among the world's top 10, according to reporting cited by The Next Web[^9]. It also covers AI agents for sensitive uses like defence, and the know-how to design some advanced AI and memory chips[^8][^9]. Open-source code and published research are exempt, and Chinese companies could still serve foreign users through apps and websites[^9]. Public comments are open until November 15, and firms must already register before exporting listed items[^9].

Background: for years the US has blocked China from buying the most advanced AI chips and chipmaking machines[^8]. Now China is using similar tools on its own technology. A commerce ministry spokesperson called the move "necessary" for national security and said it aims to keep AI "under human control"; the ministry says it does not target any country[^8][^9].

Why it matters: Chinese AI models are popular abroad because they are cheap and often free to download. One analyst told AP the rules are a response to Western demands for control over key technologies, and another said access to technology is becoming more split between blocs[^8]. My read: if the final rules are strict, companies outside China may find it harder to run the biggest Chinese models on their own computers.

topics.heading: UN calls for an end to drone strikes in Sudan as famine risk grows
topics.summary: At the UN Security Council, a senior UN official said drones are now the leading cause of civilian deaths in Sudan's war and urged a mutual ban. Sudan's army-led government opposed widening the arms embargo.

lead.title: UN demands immediate end to drone attacks in Sudan as civilian deaths mount

alsoReported.title: Security Council LIVE: Sudan's war spreads as drones and hunger take a deadly toll

article: On Friday, the UN Security Council met on Sudan, where the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group, have fought since April 2023. UN political chief Rosemary DiCarlo said drones have become the leading cause of civilian casualties this year, and that a mutual ban on them could "dramatically improve" protection for civilians[^10]. UN data show more than 1,100 people were killed by drone strikes in the first half of 2026[^10].

DiCarlo said neither side is moving toward talks, because each believes it can still gain on the battlefield with outside support[^10][^12]. Britain called for tougher sanctions on people who supply and fund the fighting, and the US called for a humanitarian truce and a wider arms embargo[^10]. Recent strikes include an attack on a displacement shelter in Blue Nile state; a US diplomat said it was reportedly carried out by the RSF[^10].

The hunger crisis is deepening. About 20 million people face acute hunger, according to UN figures[^11]. A UN-backed hunger monitor warned on October 12 that drought linked to El Niño, on top of the war, is pushing parts of Darfur and Kordofan toward famine, and that the aid appeal is less than half funded[^13].

Why it matters: the UN calls Sudan the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis[^11]. More than 700,000 displaced people in the town of Tawila alone are short of food, water and health care[^11]. The arms embargo still covers only Darfur, and sanctions run to December 11[^11]. My read: without pressure on the outside suppliers of drones and weapons, a UN call alone is unlikely to change much.
topics.differences: Sudan's UN representative said any truce requires the RSF to leave towns it holds, and opposed expanding the arms embargo; Russia, Egypt and Pakistan warned that sanctions should not weaken Sudan's state institutions, while the US and UK want wider sanctions[^12][^10]. Ethiopia said reports indicate a neighbouring state ran drone strikes inside Sudan[^12].

topics.heading: Ten days before Israel votes, polls show no clear majority for either bloc
topics.summary: Israel holds a general election on October 27. A Maariv poll has former army chief Gadi Eisenkot ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as preferred leader, but neither bloc near the 61 seats needed to govern.

lead.title: The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu

alsoReported.title: Israelis prefer unity gov't to another election, Benjamin Netanyahu falls behind Gadi Eisenkot

article: Israelis vote on October 27 for all 120 seats in the Knesset, their parliament. A party leader becomes prime minister by putting together a coalition with at least 61 seats[^15]. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces five main rivals who signed a pact in September to avoid attacking each other and to try to replace him[^14].

A poll by Lazar Research for the Maariv newspaper, taken October 14 and 15, found 48% preferred Gadi Eisenkot as prime minister and 41% Netanyahu[^15]. It projected Eisenkot's new Yashar party as the largest with 21 seats, but both Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition bloc at 51 seats each, with Arab parties holding 14[^15]. That is one poll from one firm, so treat it as a snapshot rather than a forecast; Israeli polls have often missed by a few seats, and a few seats decide who can govern (my read).

Al Jazeera notes the opposition is not mainly left-wing[^14]. Eisenkot, a former army chief, and Naftali Bennett, who leads a joint list with Yair Lapid, take broadly right-leaning security positions; only Yair Golan's Democrats mention a Palestinian state, and only as a distant goal[^14]. Most opposition leaders rule out governing with Arab parties, which makes reaching 61 seats harder[^14].

Why it matters: the result will shape how Israel handles the stalled Gaza truce, Lebanon and the war with Iran[^14]. Most Israelis in the Maariv poll said they would prefer a unity government over another election if the result is unclear[^15]. My read: the likeliest outcome is weeks of coalition bargaining rather than a quick winner.

question.text: The US and Iran give opposite accounts of Hormuz, and France's government and unions counted very different crowds. When the people giving a number have a stake in it, what would you check before deciding which figure to trust?
